title: ASIC issues stop orders against trio of private-lending funds
full_text:
The Australian Securities & Investments Commission has halted three private-lending schemes over concerns retail investors were being misled over issues such as the loan portfolios and the cost of an exit.
ASIC issued interim stop orders on three managed investment schemes run by the Australian Secure Capital Fund, preventing the fund from offering, issuing, selling or transferring interests in its ASCF Premium Capital Fund, the ASCF Select Income Fund and the ASCF High Yield Fund.
The three schemes, which invest in short-term mortgages, including bridging loans, have about $250m in funds under management – all from retail investors.
Australian Secure Capital Fund has been operating since 2016 and targets distribution rates of 6.35 per cent to 7.75 per cent per annum, and has investment terms from three to 24 months.
ASIC’s concerns were that the product disclosure statement failed to disclose information about the funds’ loan portfolio, that the document might have included a misleading and deceptive statement and that it omitted information about the cost of selling out of the fund.
“Firms must ensure their disclosures to investors are transparent and support informed decision making, including to help investors understand the strategies and risks of their products,” ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said.
“As foreshadowed in all our work in the private credit space, where ASIC identifies disclosure concerns we will act swiftly to protect investors from potential harm and promote higher standards across the sector.” ASIC increased its surveillance of the under-pressure private-credit sector last year.
The private-credit sector faces increased scrutiny from both investors and regulators amid fears of growing liquidity and valuation risks. The country’s biggest non-bank commercial lender, Metrics Credit Partners, which has about $20bn in client funds under management, was this month forced to suspend its funds amid a dispute with auditor KPMG over its asset valuations.
After eventually conceding to the lower valuations pushed by KPMG, Metrics’ three ASX-listed funds this week were back trading following a short-term suspension. But its unlisted funds are still closed to investors.
Metrics chief executive Andrew Lockhart on Wednesday said his firm would undertake a review of its governance processes following the damaging stand-off with KPMG, and he raised the possibility of remediation for investors in the fund.
The prudential regulator, meanwhile, last week warned of heightened risks in the nation’s $4.5 trillion retirement pot from private credit. Super fund Insignia Financial has a $4.5bn exposure to Metrics, while others including Australian Retirement Trust, Rest Super and Care Super also have positions in the private credit operator.
